961.event_title: Muhammad Ali refuses induction into the United States Army
961.event: On 28 April 1967 the heavyweight boxing champion Muhammad Ali appeared for induction into the United States Army in Houston and refused to step forward when his name was called, citing his religious beliefs as a conscientious objector. Boxing authorities suspended his licence and stripped him of his title, and he was convicted of refusing induction and sentenced to five years in prison, though he remained free on appeal. He was kept out of the ring for more than three years before the Supreme Court unanimously overturned his conviction in Clay v. United States in June 1971.
961.explanation: Ali gave up his title and his best years as a boxer rather than act against what he held to be his conscience.
961.tie_back: The kural says that even acts one seems unable to live without must be given up if doing them would lower one's dignity, and Ali sacrificed the career that was his livelihood rather than do what he believed was wrong.
961._accuracy_note: Strong fit to giving up something indispensable for the sake of self-respect; the kural's framing in terms of family honour is not present.

962.event_title: Lawrence Lemieux stops racing to rescue rival sailors at the Seoul Olympics
962.place: Off Busan, South Korea (1988 Seoul Olympic Games)
962.event: During a Finn-class race at the 1988 Olympic sailing regatta, held in strong winds off Busan, Canadian sailor Lawrence Lemieux was running in second place overall when he saw that two sailors from Singapore had been thrown from their capsized boat. He left the course, pulled the injured sailors from the water and stayed with them until a patrol boat arrived, then rejoined the race and finished far back, losing his chance of a medal. The International Olympic Committee awarded him the Pierre de Coubertin Medal for sportsmanship.
962.explanation: Lemieux showed that an Olympic medal was worth less to him than doing what was right by other competitors in danger.
962.tie_back: The kural says those who want true nobility will not do anything unworthy even if it would win them fame, and Lemieux would not sail on toward a medal while others were in danger.
962._accuracy_note: Strong fit to placing worthiness above fame; his final placing varies between sources, so it is not stated.

963.event_title: Albert Einstein declines the presidency of Israel
963.event: After Chaim Weizmann, Israel's first president, died on 9 November 1952, Ambassador Abba Eban wrote to Albert Einstein on behalf of Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion to ask whether he would accept the presidency if the Knesset elected him. Einstein declined within days, replying that he was deeply moved by the offer but lacked the natural aptitude and experience to deal with people and carry out official duties. Yitzhak Ben-Zvi was elected president instead.
963.explanation: At the height of his world fame, Einstein turned down a head of state's office with a modest account of his own limits.
963.tie_back: The kural asks for humility when fortune swells, and Einstein answered the greatest honour offered to him by declaring himself unfit for it.
963._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit to the first half of the kural (humility in good fortune); the second half, standing tall in hardship, is not illustrated.

964.event_title: Puyi, the last emperor of China, works at the Beijing Botanical Garden
964.event: Puyi had become emperor of China as a small child, abdicated in 1912, and later served as the Japanese-backed ruler of Manchukuo; after years of imprisonment he was pardoned in December 1959. He was then assigned work at the Beijing Botanical Garden, where he lived among ordinary workers. He later worked as a researcher for a national historical committee, published an autobiography, and died in Beijing in 1967.
964.explanation: Puyi's life is one of history's sharpest falls, from a throne regarded as sacred to an ordinary job in a public garden.
964.tie_back: The kural says people who fall from their high station become like hair fallen from the head, prized while in place and ordinary once fallen, and Puyi's later life showed that change.
964._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit to a fall from high station, but Puyi fell mainly through revolution and war rather than through a loss of honour, which is the kural's point.

965.event_title: Diego Maradona is sent home from the 1994 World Cup
965.place: Foxborough, Massachusetts, United States (1994 FIFA World Cup)
965.event: Diego Maradona, captain of Argentina and one of the most celebrated footballers in history, failed a drug test after a World Cup match against Nigeria on 25 June 1994, when laboratory analysis found ephedrine-related stimulants in his sample. He was withdrawn from the tournament, and in August 1994 FIFA banned him from football for 15 months. Maradona denied taking the substance intentionally, saying he had taken a replacement diet product; he never played in a World Cup again.
965.explanation: One failed test, involving a substance far smaller in scale than his achievements, ended the World Cup career of a national hero and became the lasting image of his final tournament.
965.tie_back: The kural says that even people as great as a mountain are brought low by a debasing act no bigger than a kunri seed, and Maradona's fall came from a few traces of a banned stimulant.
965._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit to a great figure brought low by a small offence; Maradona disputed that the offence was deliberate, and the entry reflects that.

966.event_title: Samuel Johnson's letter to Lord Chesterfield
966.event: Lord Chesterfield had accepted the dedication of Samuel Johnson's plan for a Dictionary of the English Language in 1747 but gave the project almost no further help during the long years Johnson spent compiling it. Shortly before the Dictionary appeared in 1755, Chesterfield published two magazine articles praising it, creating the impression that he had been its patron all along. On 7 February 1755 Johnson wrote to him rejecting his belated patronage, and copies of the letter circulated among Johnson's circle and were later printed by James Boswell.
966.explanation: The letter became famous as a declaration of an author's independence from aristocratic patronage.
966.tie_back: The kural asks what is gained by trailing after those who scorn you, and Johnson refused to attach himself to a patron who had neglected him once his success made the patron eager.
966._accuracy_note: Close fit: Johnson declines to follow after one who had disregarded him.

967.event_title: Arturo Toscanini refuses to serve the Fascist and Nazi regimes
967.place: Bologna, Italy; Bayreuth, Germany; Salzburg, Austria
967.event: On 14 May 1931 the conductor Arturo Toscanini refused to open a memorial concert in Bologna with the Fascist anthem Giovinezza, and was struck by a group of Fascist youths outside the theatre; his passport was later taken away for a time. In 1933 he withdrew from the Bayreuth Festival in protest at Nazi treatment of Jewish musicians, and in 1938 he broke with the Salzburg Festival as Austria came under Hitler's control. He refused to conduct in Italy while the Fascist regime lasted and went to the United States, returning to conduct at the rebuilt La Scala in 1946.
967.explanation: Toscanini gave up the leading stages of Europe and his own country rather than lend his art to regimes he opposed.
967.tie_back: The kural says it is better to be called ruined than to live by trailing after those who do not value you, and Toscanini chose exile over serving rulers who demanded his submission.
967._accuracy_note: Strong fit to refusing to live as a follower of those who scorn one's values; he did not face ruin, as he prospered in America.

968.event_title: Dietrich Bonhoeffer returns to Germany from New York
968.place: New York, United States, and Berlin, Germany
968.event: In June 1939 the German pastor and theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer, an opponent of the Nazi regime, accepted an offer from friends to come to Union Theological Seminary in New York, which would have kept him safe abroad. Within weeks he decided that his place was in Germany and sailed home in July 1939, shortly before the outbreak of war. He joined the resistance to Hitler, was arrested in 1943, and was executed at Flossenburg concentration camp on 9 April 1945.
968.explanation: Bonhoeffer judged that a safe life abroad would cost him his integrity and his right to help rebuild Germany after the war.
968.tie_back: The kural asks whether a life that merely keeps the body going is any medicine against death when one's dignity is at stake, and Bonhoeffer gave up safety rather than live with that loss.
968._accuracy_note: Strong fit to choosing honour over mere survival; the event illustrates the choice, not the kural's philosophical argument about death.

969.event_title: The soldiers of HMS Birkenhead stand fast as the ship sinks
969.place: Danger Point, near Gansbaai, South Africa
969.event: The troopship HMS Birkenhead, carrying soldiers and some of their families to the Eastern Cape, struck rocks off Danger Point on 26 February 1852. With only a few lifeboats usable, the officers ordered the soldiers to stand fast rather than rush the boats and swamp them, and the men kept their ranks on deck as the ship went down. All the women and children aboard were saved, but about 445 of the 638 people on board were lost, and the soldiers' conduct gave rise to the phrase the Birkenhead drill.
969.explanation: The soldiers' discipline became a lasting example of putting honour and duty above one's own survival, and helped establish the rule of women and children first.
969.tie_back: The kural says people of honour would give up life itself rather than lose their honour, and the Birkenhead soldiers held their ranks to the end rather than save themselves at others' cost.
969._accuracy_note: Strong fit to valuing honour above life; the soldiers acted under orders and to save others, which is nobler than, though not identical to, the kural's image.

970.event_title: Rani Lakshmi Bai of Jhansi is honoured as a national heroine
970.event: After the death of her husband, the ruler of Jhansi, the British East India Company refused to recognise their adopted son as heir and annexed the state in 1854, rejecting Lakshmi Bai's petition to rule as regent. During the rebellion of 1857-58 she led the defence of Jhansi, escaped when the city fell in April 1858, joined other leaders in taking Gwalior, and was killed in combat near Gwalior in June 1858. Her British opponent, General Hugh Rose, called her the bravest and best of the rebel leaders, and she became a symbol of courage in India, honoured in poetry, statues and the names of institutions.
970.explanation: Lakshmi Bai's refusal to accept the loss of her state and her son's rights made her one of the most revered figures in Indian history.
970.tie_back: The kural says the world forever honours those who would not go on living in disgrace, and India's lasting reverence for the Rani of Jhansi shows exactly that.
970._accuracy_note: Strong fit to lasting fame for refusing dishonour; her birth year and exact date of death vary between sources and are not stated.
